query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, localized surface segregation that enriches the nanoparticle surface in lower–melting point elements (e.g., copper and nickel) creates regions of reduced cohesive energy that act as nucleation sites for premelting. This results in an overall reduction and broadening of the premelting temperature range compared to compositionally homogeneous nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, homogeneous iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with a uniform BCC or FCC-like solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a mild annealing treatment prior to high-temperature testing to induce controlled surface segregation, compared to as-cast (unmodified) nanoparticles.
generation.conditions: Nanoparticles (ideally below ~20–30 nm diameter) are subjected to in situ heating experiments under high-vacuum or inert gas environments, with controlled temperature ramps crossing the premelting and melting regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of a chemically heterogeneous surface layer due to surface segregation of lower–melting point species, altering the local bonding environment at the nanoparticle surfaces.
generation.mechanism: The segregation creates regions of lower cohesive energy at the nanoparticle surfaces, which facilitates the nucleation of a liquid-like layer (premelting) at temperatures below the bulk melting point of the homogeneous phase. This effect, combined with the high surface-to-volume ratio in nanoparticles, modulates the premelting and melting behavior by reducing the effective energy barrier for phase transition at the surfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that have undergone the segregation-inducing annealing treatment will exhibit earlier onset of surface premelting (shifted by tens of Kelvin) and a broader melting transition relative to the unmodified, homogeneous nanoparticles. Differential scanning calorimetry and in situ TEM heating experiments will reveal a lower premelting temperature and more gradual melting for the surface-segregated particles.
generation.baseline: Homogeneous iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles without any induced surface segregation treatment.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected in nanoparticles where the size is sufficiently small for surface effects to dominate (approximately <20–30 nm) and for compositions where the elemental differences in melting points and surface energies are significant enough to drive segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the temperature shift and the degree of broadening in the melting transition are uncertain due to the interplay of nanoparticle size, stoichiometry, and kinetic factors during segregation; quantitative values are likely system dependent.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles with identical size distributions. Subject one batch to a mild annealing treatment designed to promote surface segregation and leave the other batch untreated. Perform in situ TEM heating experiments coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) on both batches to monitor changes in surface composition and melting behavior.
measurements: Temperature at onset of observable surface premelting via in situ TEM imaging
EDS composition profiles at the nanoparticle surfaces versus cores
Melting peak shifts and latent heat changes measured by DSC
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (segregated) nanoparticles do not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., >10 K) decrease in the onset temperature of premelting and do not show broader melting transitions compared to the untreated (homogeneous) nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that surface segregation governs the premelting and melting behavior is falsified.

Paper card. Question: How can the computational cost of calculating ab initio melting properties for multi-component high-entropy alloys be reduced while maintaining sub-meV accuracy?. System: TaVCrW high-entropy alloy (bcc refractory). Processing: A hierarchical approach combining EAM potentials, Moment Tensor Potentials (MTP), and Density Functional Theory (DFT) using Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) to replace thermodynamic integration (TI); specifically, an optimized MTP replaces one EAM potential and TI is replaced by FEP for the liquid free energy calculation.. Test conditions: GGA-PBE and LDA exchange-correlation functionals; temperatures ranging from 2200 K to 2500 K; volumes on a 5 × 6 (V, T) grid; comparison against CALPHAD extrapolated values and original TOR-TILD method..
